taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Nassella leucotricha; older Texas literature commonly uses Stipa leucotricha.
look_here_first: COOL-SEASON winter-green clump first: Texas wintergrass often greens during winter while warm-season grasses brown. At bloom in spring, the panicle is loose or somewhat narrowed with distinct long-awned individual spikelets, as the new Sam Kieschnick photo shows. Crucially, FOLLOW ONE mature floret to its ONE long, twisted and twice-bent awn attached to a hard lemma, then verify a long sharp hairy callus at the opposite base. The USDA example arrows show the callus, lemma and awn of ONE fruit. Nearby Aristida has THREE awn limbs from one lemma; cultivated Mexican feathergrass also has a single awn but a tiny blunt callus and thinner rolled foliage.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Flora of Purola Preserve, N. Hays County explicitly records Nassella leucotricha. Travis — Travis County environmental documentation explicitly records Texas wintergrass (Nassella leucotricha) in native grassland/woodland vegetation; Barton Creek Habitat Preserve research also lists it as a dominant herbaceous species in Travis County. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County provides a detailed treatment under the synonym Stipa leucotricha.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: No county occurrence inferred from statewide or ecoregion distribution alone.

best_field_traits: COOL SEASON: Texas wintergrass grows green and actively through fall, winter and early spring, sometimes when little bluestem and KR are tan; seasonal timing is support, not a stand-alone species ID.
PANICLE: loose open flowering branches bearing individual one-flowered spikelets, unlike Aristida's familiar three terminal awns and little bluestem's many short separate silky racemes.
FLORET: each narrow, hardened fertile lemma has ONE long twisted, usually twice-bent AWN (often ~40–90 mm); do not count awns from DIFFERENT spikelets.
SHARP SEED BASE: a long pointed, often hairy CALLUS forms the speargrass barb; handle dry seeds carefully and inspect under magnification.
CROWN/NECK: near the awn insertion, the mature lemma has a pale membranous apical crown/neck, commonly with a ring of hairs, visible with a strong hand lens.
GLUMES: two persistent pale, often oatlike bracts around the developing floret, roughly 10–21 mm in FNA; after fruit drops, empty whitish glumes may remain.
LEAF: rough dark-green narrow blades with short stiff whitish hairs, culm nodes usually somewhat hairy; leaf collar often has lateral tufts of short hairs.
DON'T CONFUSE: Mexican feathergrass (Nassella tenuissima) is also one-awned but has a very fine hairlike rolled blade, generally smaller/flimsier florets and a far SHORTER blunter callus.
Additional clue for field season: Texas wintergrass may form self-pollinating cleistogenous florets in basal leaf sheaths; these alone do not identify a sterile plant.
morphology_keys.joey_family_training: Poaceae family training: identify inflorescence architecture first, then inspect spikelets/glumes/lemma-palea/awns and ligule-collar-sheath characters.
morphology_keys.habit: Cool-season perennial tufted bunchgrass, often conspicuously green in winter in open native Central Texas grassland; can be up to 1.2 m tall in fruiting shoots.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Open to sometimes rather contracted slender panicle, generally bearing well-spaced one-flowered spikelets rather than Aristida's trifid awn per lemma; FNA describes terminal panicles 5–55 cm with 1–4 spikelets on branchlets.
morphology_keys.fruit: Mature dry fruit enveloped by a hardened linear lemma terminating below in a pointed often hairy callus (~1–5.5 mm FNA); one rope-twisted twice-bent awn (~40–90 mm FNA, more variable across other Texas treatments) extends above a collar/crown. These sharp diaspores can penetrate skin, clothing and livestock tissue. Avoid handling without care.
morphology_keys.collars_and_ligules: Leaf blades rough from whitish bristles; sheaths may be hairy. Collars may show lateral short-hair tufts and brown/purple shading; membranous ligule often ~0.2–1.2 mm (FNA). Compare with broad Poaceae anatomical glossary if no macro.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Aristida (oldfield and purple threeawn): THREE terminal lemma awn branches from ONE floret, rather than Nassella leucotricha's SINGLE awn. Mexican feathergrass N. tenuissima: ALSO has ONE long awn, but tightly hairlike rolled leaves, much SMALLER fertile lemma (~1.8–3.6 mm versus N. leucotricha ~5.3–13 mm across major descriptions), and a very short blunt callus (~0.2–0.4 mm vs leucotricha usually >1 mm). Little bluestem: warm-season with many short silky separate racemes along upper leafy branches, not a loose wintergreen needlegrass panicle. Canada and Virginia wildrye: cool-season grasses too, but bear multiple awned spikelets clustered into more obvious spikes; inspect floret awn placement and entire inflorescence.

field_matrix.taxon: Purple / oldfield threeawn — Aristida purpurea / A. oligantha
field_matrix.where_to_look: Select one intact FERTILE LEMMA and count awns arising from that very same floret.
field_matrix.this_species: Texas wintergrass: ONE rope-twisted, often twice-bent, long awn attached to ONE hardened, sharp-callused lemma; loose winter/spring flowering panicle.
field_matrix.look_alike: Aristida: THREE spreading awn BRANCHES extend from ONE lemma; many threeawns are warm-season and share wiry grass habit.
field_matrix.quick_rule: One awn on a sharply pointed needlegrass lemma favors Nassella; three awn tips from one lemma points to Aristida. Detached awns without attachment cannot decide.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Inspect actual mature lemma, callus and leaf blade width with 1-mm scale.
field_matrix.this_species: Wintergrass has a larger floret/lemma (~5.3–13 mm depending treatment), longer sharp hairy callus (about 1.2–5.5 mm in Flora of North America), rough blades usually 1–3.6 mm wide, and a pale corona/neck.
field_matrix.look_alike: Mexican feathergrass is a dense soft fine-hairlike clump with extremely narrow tightly rolled leaves (often ≤0.5 mm), much smaller lemma (~1.8–3.6 mm) and short ~0.2–0.4 mm rather blunt callus; its awn can ALSO be very long.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Do not use ONE awn alone. A noticeably elongate sharp callus and larger lemma support N. leucotricha; tiny short blunt callus + filamentous leaf supports N. tenuissima.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Trace an attached flowering stalk and record whether the specimen was green through winter.
field_matrix.this_species: Cool-season perennial, open needlegrass panicle, one twisted awn per hard pointed fruit; basal photos show narrow rough green blades.
field_matrix.look_alike: Warm-season little bluestem repeatedly carries individual SHORT silky racemes at different upper leafy branch tips; fall bronze color is supporting only.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Wintergreen bunch with one-awned individual fruit and loose flowering panicle favors wintergrass; many separate upper short silky racemes favors little.

field_matrix.taxon: Canada / Virginia wildrye — Elymus canadensis / E. virginicus
field_matrix.where_to_look: Check whether spikelets crowd onto a single conspicuous terminal SPIKE (wheatlike) or form a branching open PANICLE.
field_matrix.this_species: Nassella has open/loose or narrow panicle of more isolated ONE-flowered spikelets and long single twisting awns on hard fruit.
field_matrix.look_alike: Elymus wildryes have multiple spikelets at successive axis nodes in terminal spikes; longer awns can give a bristly silhouette but the flowering architecture differs.
field_matrix.quick_rule: A conspicuous wheat/rye-like spike of multiple spikelets is not the loose individual-flowered Nassella panicle.

not_reliable_alone: Number of awns visible across the ENTIRE seedhead: count only those on one intact lemma.
Green winter growth, by itself; many other native cool-season grasses remain green.
Long awn length alone, since Mexican feathergrass also has a long awn.
Pale oatlike empty glumes when actual fruit has shed, without a same-plant mature floret.
Purple, gold or straw grass color or a graceful clump silhouette.
Detached long awn, or sharp fruit without intact glumes and stem, when source identity is uncertain.

visual_comparison.title: Texas wintergrass — green tuft → awned head → sharp single-awed fruit
visual_comparison.subtitle: Two formerly unused local archived CC BY JPEGs now directly teach wintergreen bunch and living awned flowering head, paired with public-domain USDA single-lemma sharp callus + one twisted awn. Threeawn and Mexican feathergrass panels explicitly DIFFERENT species. Fine collar and measured crown photo gaps remain.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: Start with cool-season green bunch, THEN open spring panicle; trace ONE attached mature floret. One long twice-bent twisted AWN and an elongated sharp hairy CALLUS support Texas wintergrass. THREE limbs from one lemma = Aristida. One awn alone does not exclude Mexican feathergrass.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Field sequence — actual winter bunch, spring awned head, one HARD point
steps: 1. In winter or early spring, FIND the actual green bunch like photo 1 (CC BY John Thomlinson). It is not unique enough to identify this grass alone.

2. At flowering, photograph a COMPLETE head from that same individual: photo 2 (CC BY Sam Kieschnick) shows narrow attached floral units and long threadlike awns among thin branches. Avoid guessing awn count from a whole head.

3. Select ONE mature FERTILE LEMMA, not an empty glume or another fruit: USDA image photo 3 has precise verified arrows for SHARP HAIRY CALLUS at its base, HARD LEMMA BODY and ONE rope-twisted awn above.
4. Compare Aristida: three terminal awn LIMBS depart from the SAME individual lemma. Other long awns in the photo may belong to other florets.
5. Compare Mexican feathergrass N. tenuissima: it also has one long awn, but the mature lemma and especially the CALLUS are substantially smaller/blunter; photograph and measure actual adult fruits.

6. When safe, use hand lens to inspect 0.2–1.2 mm SHORT membranous ligule, 0.75–2 mm pale flared crown/neck beneath awn, and 1–5.5 mm sharp often hairy callus (Flora of North America treatment, individual measured specimens vary). All still lack verified high-resolution same-plant local teaching photos.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Visible gross photos: winter-active bunch -> attached often loose spring flowering head. ID requires one mature floret with ONE long bent/twisted awn and an elongated sharp callus; one-awed Mexican feathergrass remains a lookalike. Threeawns have THREE limbs on ONE lemma, not three nearby separated florets.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: New John Thomlinson and Sam Kieschnick archive JPEGs are recorded CC BY and physically installed already; genus/species source view now reuses them with full source credit. Neither shows an individual measured lemma/corona/collar. Archived CC BY version needs eventual photo-level license recheck. USDA detached fruit image is public domain but non-Hays; Abilene CC BY-NC is restricted to credited noncommercial deployment. Keep individual rights and county nativity determinations unchanged.

field_id_finish_pass.priority: One-awed pointed fruit vs threeawn plus Mexican feathergrass callus contrast; source-permitted photo-first teaching.
first_field_sequence: Look for native Texas wintergrass active green in late fall to early spring as a cool-season bunch.
Trace one flowing panicle to an intact SINGLE-flowered spikelet, not simply a handful of awns.
Count lemma AWNS from ONE fertile floret: ONE extremely long twisted and bent strand implies needlegrass; THREE arms implies Aristida.
Under magnification, locate the POINTED seed CALLUS and pale CROWN at the top of the Nassella lemma; document fruit dimensions.
Check whether Mexican feathergrass could fit: very tiny narrow leaves and very short blunt callus in N. tenuissima.
If only empty glumes or loose seedhead remains, use Nassella sp. / needlegrass candidate until mature fruit confirms.

remaining_macro_photo_targets: Same rooted Hays County verified Texas wintergrass, alive in winter and flowering spring, comparable scale
Same-plant short MEMBRANOUS ligule at blade/sheath junction, lens and metric scale
Actual separated adult lemma with sharp hairy callus measured in millimeters (FNA 1–5.5mm, taxonomic ranges vary)
Pale distal corona/crown just below ONE awn with mm scale, diagnostic for Nassella and not visible in current gross photos
Whole attached glumes, lemma and awn in one calibrated frame; separate one-flowered spikelet from the grass panicle
Same-scale mature N. tenuissima smaller short blunt callus comparison (one-awed too); compare THREE-awed Aristida mature lemma
field_id_finish_pass.quality_label: Six directly inspected gross-anatomy arrows across 2 physically present CC BY archived JPEGs (three arrows: wintergreen tuft and live flowering head) and the existing USDA public-domain one-floret fruit reference (three arrows: sharp hairy callus, hardened lemma body, one rope-twisted awn). Color and habit alone are not IDs; no macro scale or independent Hays voucher is claimed.
